## Where This Fits
This is the only week of pre-Transformer NLP in the course, so it is deliberately restrained: rather than a full tour of what came before, **each component is introduced through the specific failure it was built to fix**. The point is that when the Transformer arrives you can put a finger on each of its design choices and name the earlier pain it answers. The last link in that chain of failures — words that are not in the vocabulary at all — is what hands you over to tokenization in W2.

It is also where the course's governing metaphor — **compression is prediction** — is set up, to be used again every few weeks. Two items that belong to no single unit are introduced here as well: the compute ledger, and the four questions to put to any paper. This week you work out the ledger's training-side number; its memory-side number, the KV cache, opens W3, because it needs attention heads to mean something first.

## Learning Objectives
1. Write down the MLE estimate for an n-gram language model and the definition of perplexity, and use Zipf–Heaps and Good-Turing to explain why sparsity **cannot be fixed with any affordable amount of data**: the probability mass of unseen events does fall as the corpus grows, but the rate at which it falls goes to zero as $n$ grows — which leaves only the inductive bias of smoothing or backoff, or parameter sharing.
2. Explain how the distributional hypothesis is made concrete by the word2vec objective (skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorizes a shifted PMI matrix), and diagnose three structural failures of static embeddings: the senses of a polysemous word are stacked into one vector, antonyms sit close together under cosine, and a word outside the vocabulary has no vector at all.
3. Identify the multiplied gradients of backpropagation through time in an RNN and the fixed-length bottleneck of the encoder-decoder; say which specific symptom of the bottleneck attention was proposed against (translation quality collapsing as sentences get longer); and compare recurrence with attention on **training parallelism, inference memory, and recall from context**.
4. Use cross-entropy and bits-per-byte to argue that a language model is a compressor, and say where that equivalence breaks down — including the conditions under which bits-per-byte is actually comparable, and how *compressing a distribution rather than a set of facts* leads, statistically, to hallucination.
5. Use $C \approx 6ND$ to estimate the training compute of a dense model at a compute-optimal configuration, and convert it into time on a single consumer GPU.

## References
- **JM3** Ch 3 *N-gram Language Models* (**the whole chapter** — §3.7, on how perplexity relates to entropy, comes last and is the core of this week's compression argument), Ch 5 *Embeddings* (§5.1–5.5), Ch 6 *Neural Networks* (the feedforward neural language model subsection under §6.5, which is the NPLM), and Ch 14 *RNNs and LSTMs* (§14.1–14.2 and §14.5, plus **§14.7–14.8 on the encoder-decoder and attention** — they sit at the end of the chapter, so do not stop halfway)
- **UDL** ch 1–2 (the catch-up route for students with no background); **BB** for the probability and optimization assumed here
- **ZZM** ch 5 *Basic Language Models* (n-grams, smoothing, PPL, FNN-LM, LSTM-LM) and ch 3 *Distributed Representation* (CBOW / skip-gram / ELMo) — **these two chapters are very nearly the skeleton of this week, and the book is open access, so it can be handed out directly**; take the first half of ch 4 as well for the closing stretch (seq2seq → attention), and add ch 2 *Basics of Neural Network* if the background is missing
- Shannon, **A Mathematical Theory of Communication**, Bell System Technical Journal 27(3):379–423 and 27(4):623–656, 1948 — generating English text by successive approximations starts here, and this week's opening demo is a re-run of it; and Shannon, **Prediction and Entropy of Printed English**, Bell System Technical Journal 30(1):50–64, 1951 — estimating the entropy of English by having people guess the next letter, which is where *compression is prediction* begins
- Bengio et al., **A Neural Probabilistic Language Model**, JMLR 2003 — the NPLM, where parameter sharing first answers sparsity
- Chen & Goodman, **An empirical study of smoothing techniques for language modeling**, Computer Speech & Language 13(4):359–393, 1999 — the systematic comparison of smoothing methods; and Kneser & Ney, **Improved backing-off for M-gram language modeling**, ICASSP 1995, vol. 1, pp. 181–184 — where Kneser-Ney smoothing comes from
- Good, **The Population Frequencies of Species and the Estimation of Population Parameters**, Biometrika 40(3–4):237–264, 1953 — where the Good-Turing estimate comes from; Church & Gale, **A comparison of the enhanced Good-Turing and deleted estimation methods for estimating probabilities of English bigrams**, Computer Speech & Language 5(1):19–54, 1991 — compares Good-Turing estimates against held-out data on English bigrams, the idea behind the check under the figure on this week's Good-Turing slide; Gale & Sampson, **Good-Turing Frequency Estimation Without Tears**, Journal of Quantitative Linguistics 2(3):217–237, 1995 — Simple Good-Turing, which smooths $N_c$ before using it, as any practical version has to
- Mikolov et al., **Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space**, arXiv:1301.3781 (2013); and **Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality**, NeurIPS 2013 — negative sampling is in the second one
- Pennington et al., **GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation**, EMNLP 2014
- Levy & Goldberg, **Neural Word Embedding as Implicit Matrix Factorization**, NeurIPS 2014 — ties skip-gram with negative sampling back to factorizing a shifted PMI matrix; the single strongest reference for the claim that an embedding's similarity is whatever its training objective defined similarity to be
- Dyer, **Notes on Noise Contrastive Estimation and Negative Sampling**, arXiv:1410.8251 (2014) — a four-page technical note rather than a peer-reviewed paper, but the clearest account of how negative sampling differs from noise-contrastive estimation, and why the former is not a general-purpose estimator
- Bojanowski et al., **Enriching Word Vectors with Subword Information**, TACL (arXiv:1607.04606) — fastText, which builds a vector for an out-of-vocabulary word from its character n-grams; the prequel to W2
- Arora et al., **Linear Algebraic Structure of Word Senses, with Applications to Polysemy**, TACL 2018 (arXiv:1601.03764) — the several senses of a word sit in linear superposition inside a single word vector
- Peters et al., **Deep contextualized word representations**, NAACL 2018 (arXiv:1802.05365) — ELMo; contextual embeddings are what fix the polysemy failure
- Ethayarajh, **How Contextual are Contextualized Word Representations? Comparing the Geometry of BERT, ELMo, and GPT-2 Embeddings**, EMNLP 2019 (arXiv:1909.00512) — contextual representations are not isotropic in any layer, and a static embedding explains on average less than 5% of their variance; the first point comes back when W12 looks at cosine similarity
- Bengio, Simard & Frasconi, **Learning Long-Term Dependencies with Gradient Descent is Difficult**, IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks 5(2):157–166, 1994 — an early source for the multiplied-gradient argument
- Pascanu, Mikolov & Bengio, **On the difficulty of training Recurrent Neural Networks**, arXiv:1211.5063 (2012) — states sufficient and necessary conditions for vanishing and exploding gradients in terms of singular values, and proposes gradient-norm clipping
- Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, **Long Short-Term Memory**, Neural Computation 9(8):1735–1780, 1997 — the original LSTM, whose constant error carousel is a genuinely additive path
- Gers, Schmidhuber & Cummins, **Learning to Forget: Continual Prediction with LSTM**, Neural Computation 12(10):2451–2471, 2000 — adds the forget gate, giving the LSTM in use today
- Srivastava, Greff & Schmidhuber, **Highway Networks**, ICML 2015 Deep Learning Workshop (arXiv:1505.00387); and He et al., **Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition**, arXiv:1512.03385 (2015) — gated and then plain identity paths across layers; the prequel to the residual stream in W4
- Sutskever, Vinyals & Le, **Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks**, NeurIPS 2014
- Cho et al., **On the Properties of Neural Machine Translation: Encoder-Decoder Approaches**, SSST-8, 2014 (arXiv:1409.1259) — encoder-decoder translation quality degrades rapidly as sentences get longer and unknown words become more frequent: the concrete symptom of the bottleneck
- Bahdanau, Cho & Bengio, **Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate**, ICLR 2015 (arXiv:1409.0473)
- Luong, Pham & Manning, **Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation**, EMNLP 2015 (arXiv:1508.04025) — the dot and general forms of attention, two years before the Transformer
- Melis, Dyer & Blunsom, **On the State of the Art of Evaluation in Neural Language Models**, arXiv:1707.05589 (2017) — properly regularized standard LSTMs outperform more recent architectures; a case study for the first of the four reading questions
- Arora et al., **Zoology: Measuring and Improving Recall in Efficient Language Models**, arXiv:2312.04927 (2023); and Jelassi et al., **Repeat After Me: Transformers are Better than State Space Models at Copying**, arXiv:2402.01032 (2024) — what a fixed-size state costs in recall and copying, and why the hybrids in W6 keep some attention
- Feng et al., **Were RNNs All We Needed?**, arXiv:2410.01201 (2024) — simplified LSTMs and GRUs that are fully parallelizable during training; a prequel to W6
- Delétang et al., **Language Modeling Is Compression**, arXiv:2309.10668 (2023) — turns *compression is prediction* into something measurable, and separates the compression rate that ignores the model's own size from the one that counts it. The course's governing metaphor has a paper behind it
- Huang et al., **Compression Represents Intelligence Linearly**, COLM 2024 (arXiv:2404.09937) — across 31 public models, average benchmark scores track compression ability almost linearly; a correlation, not a cause
- Kalai & Vempala, **Calibrated Language Models Must Hallucinate**, STOC 2024 (arXiv:2311.14648) — a calibrated model hallucinates at a rate close to the fraction of facts that appear exactly once in its training data (a Good-Turing estimate), even when that data contains no errors
- Theis, van den Oord & Bethge, **A note on the evaluation of generative models**, arXiv:1511.01844 (2015) — likelihood and sample quality are largely independent in high dimensions, with three constructed counterexamples. The reason a low perplexity does not mean good generations, and the first case study for the third of the four reading questions
- Cao & Rimell, **You should evaluate your language model on marginal likelihood over tokenisations**, EMNLP 2021 — the likelihood of the one canonical tokenization is only an upper bound on the probability of the string
- Arnett, Chang & Bergen, **A Bit of a Problem: Measurement Disparities in Dataset Sizes Across Languages**, arXiv:2403.00686 (2024) — defines the byte premium, which is why bits-per-byte cannot be compared across languages
- Liu et al., **Infini-gram: Scaling Unbounded n-gram Language Models to a Trillion Tokens**, COLM 2024 (arXiv:2401.17377); and Nguyen, **Understanding Transformers via N-gram Statistics**, NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv:2407.12034) — two new uses for n-grams in the LLM era: analysing text and memorization, and describing what an LLM predicts
- Other ways into the compression–language-modeling equivalence — search *arithmetic coding neural language model*, *bits per byte evaluation*
